aswb-bachelors-readiness-check-hgb-001.prompt: A family-preservation BSW visits a 2-year-old who insists on dressing and feeding independently, then sobs when the caregiver takes over every task to "do it right." Which Erikson stage best frames this toddler's struggle?

options.a: Autonomy versus shame and doubt in the toddler years
options.b: Integrity versus despair during late-life life review
options.c: Identity versus role confusion during adolescence
options.d: Generativity versus stagnation in midlife caregiving

aswb-bachelors-readiness-check-hgb-001.explanation: Erikson's toddler stage is autonomy versus shame and doubt: children practice self-direction (dressing, feeding, toileting) while caregivers either support safe independence or over-control and shame. A BSW uses this HBSE frame to coach the caregiver toward guided choice, not to run psychotherapy or assign a DSM label.

distractorExplanations.b: Confuses toddler autonomy with late adulthood; integrity versus despair is Erikson's last stage, not ages 1–3.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses toddler autonomy with adolescence; identity versus role confusion belongs to the teen years, not toddler self-help.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses toddler autonomy with middle adulthood; generativity versus stagnation is about guiding the next generation, not toddler self-care.

aswb-bachelors-readiness-check-hgb-002.prompt: A hospital case manager opening a three-generation file for a new dialysis patient wants to see repeating illness, caregiving, and cutoff patterns. Which tool matches that HBSE task?

options.a: An ecomap of present-day neighborhood supports and stressors
options.b: A genogram mapping family patterns across generations
options.c: A milestone chart tracking childhood developmental ages
options.d: An organizational chart of hospital social work supervision

aswb-bachelors-readiness-check-hgb-002.explanation: A genogram maps relationships, roles, illnesses, and cutoffs across at least three generations so the BSW can see repeating family patterns. It is a generalist assessment tool, not a substitute for an ecomap of current community supports or for a medical diagnosis.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses a genogram with an ecomap; ecomaps show current external supports and stressors, not multi-generation family patterns.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses a genogram with a developmental timeline; milestone charts track one child's ages, not family relationship patterns.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses a genogram with an agency org chart; genograms map the client's family system, not hospital supervision lines.

aswb-bachelors-readiness-check-hgb-003.prompt: A medical social worker plans discharge for an unhoused adult with poorly controlled diabetes who skips clinic while searching for a bed each night. Using Maslow as a motivational frame, what should the BSW prioritize?

options.a: A grief-stage worksheet about accepting the diabetes diagnosis
options.b: A psychosexual history of childhood feeding and oral conflicts
options.c: Immediate housing and food so follow-up health tasks can hold
options.d: A Piaget-style probe of abstract reasoning about insulin math

aswb-bachelors-readiness-check-hgb-003.explanation: Maslow's hierarchy is a motivational model: unmet physiological and safety needs (shelter, food) typically crowd out higher tasks such as clinic adherence. In generalist case management the BSW addresses housing and food first so diabetes self-care is even possible, without treating Maslow as a diagnosis or a therapy protocol.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses Maslow with Kübler-Ross grief stages; accepting a diagnosis is not the first motivational need when the client lacks shelter.
distractorExplanations.b: Confuses Maslow with Freud's psychosexual stages; oral-history work is not how a BSW prioritizes discharge safety needs.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses Maslow with Piaget's cognitive stages; abstract reasoning is not the barrier when nights are spent hunting for a bed.

aswb-bachelors-readiness-check-hgb-004.prompt: A school social worker meets a 7-year-old whose attendance dropped after police responded to fighting at home. The child was not struck. The teacher reports returned thumb-sucking and frequent nurse visits. What is the most accurate developmental framing?

options.a: Effects occur only if the child was also physically hit at home
options.b: School-age children typically show no effects from witnessing only
options.c: Problems stay at home, so school functioning usually stays stable
options.d: Witnessing partner violence can bring regression and school change

aswb-bachelors-readiness-check-hgb-004.explanation: Witnessing intimate-partner violence is a developmental stressor even without the child being struck. Common signs include regression, anxiety, sleep disruption, and school changes. The BSW assesses safety and functioning first and does not wait for a physical-injury threshold or a clinical diagnosis to take the impact seriously.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses exposure with direct assault; witnessing IPV alone is linked to regression, anxiety, and school problems.
distractorExplanations.b: Repeats the myth that children are unaffected as bystanders; school-age kids often show somatic complaints and skill loss.
distractorExplanations.c: Misses spillover into school; concentration, attendance, and nurse visits commonly change after home violence exposure.

aswb-bachelors-readiness-check-hgb-005.prompt: At agency intake a parent from a different faith tradition declines a mixed-gender parenting group that the program treats as standard. What does cultural humility require of the BSW first?

options.a: Do not assume agency norms are the client's; ask how they prefer to learn
options.b: Memorize a customs list for that faith and apply it to every similar client
options.c: Transfer the case so only a worker of the same culture may continue service
options.d: Treat every client identically, ignoring culture so the process stays fair

aswb-bachelors-readiness-check-hgb-005.explanation: Cultural humility is an ongoing stance: the worker does not treat agency or majority norms as the client's, and learns from this family how they prefer to receive help. NASW-aligned generalist practice asks, adapts, and reflects; it does not require a same-culture worker or a color-blind identical script.

distractorExplanations.b: Confuses humility with a static competence list; applying a faith script to every similar client stereotypes rather than asking this family.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses humility with mandatory ethnic matching; matching can be a service option, not the definition of a humble stance.
distractorExplanations.d: Describes a color-blind sameness that ignores culture; fairness here means adapting with the client, not erasing difference.

aswb-bachelors-readiness-check-hgb-006.prompt: A senior-center BSW meets a 68-year-old who entered poverty after a plant closure at 55 and later became the primary caregiver for a grandchild. Which HBSE lens best explains how timing and linked lives shape this path?

options.a: A fixed universal stage sequence every adult completes in the same order
options.b: A life-course view of historical timing, transitions, and linked lives
options.c: A single-day ecological snapshot of only today's neighborhood stressors
options.d: An unconscious childhood-conflict model that ignores later adult events

aswb-bachelors-readiness-check-hgb-006.explanation: The life-course perspective looks at historical time (plant closure), the timing of transitions (late-life poverty, unexpected caregiving), and linked lives (the grandchild). That is a better fit than a one-size stage ladder or a same-day ecomap snapshot for this aging-and-poverty story.

distractorExplanations.a: Describes rigid stage theory; life-course stresses cohort, timing, and linked lives rather than one universal adult sequence.
distractorExplanations.c: Describes a cross-sectional ecological snapshot; life-course tracks trajectories and transitions over years, not one day's stressors.
distractorExplanations.d: Describes a psychodynamic childhood-conflict frame; life-course attends to later historical events and family linkages, not the unconscious.

aswb-bachelors-readiness-check-hgb-007.prompt: A child-welfare BSW writes a plan for a 4-year-old with three foster homes in eight months who now clings, then rejects, the current caregiver. What does attachment-informed generalist practice suggest?

options.a: Rotate homes often so the child does not over-attach to one adult
options.b: Cut all birth-family contact so bonding with foster parents can start
options.c: Keep caregiving predictable and avoid extra placement moves when possible
options.d: Diagnose reactive attachment disorder today and close the case file

aswb-bachelors-readiness-check-hgb-007.explanation: Attachment disruption in care is addressed first with stable, predictable caregiving and as few additional moves as safety allows. A BSW does not diagnose attachment disorders, and planned safe family contact usually supports continuity rather than competing with foster bonding.

distractorExplanations.a: Gets attachment backwards; each extra move deepens disruption, so preventing bonds is the opposite of the treatment goal.
distractorExplanations.b: Treats birth-family contact as the enemy of bonding; safe, planned visits usually support attachment and reunification, not another loss.
distractorExplanations.d: Jumps to a DSM diagnosis a BSW does not make; disruption calls for stable caregiving first, with clinical assessment if indicated later.

aswb-bachelors-readiness-check-hgb-008.prompt: In a TANF case-management session a client leads with missed appointments and unpaid bills. Using a strengths perspective, where should the BSW start the plan?

options.a: The client's most recent medical or psychiatric diagnosis on file
options.b: The single most urgent deficit on the agency's problem checklist
options.c: The worker's preferred curriculum as the expert starting point
options.d: Resources and abilities the client already uses or can tap next

aswb-bachelors-readiness-check-hgb-008.explanation: A strengths perspective starts with what the client already has and can use—skills, relationships, past successes—then builds the plan around those resources. Deficits and diagnoses still matter for safety and eligibility, but they are not the opening frame in generalist BSW practice.

distractorExplanations.a: Starts from the medical/deficit model; strengths practice begins with abilities and resources, not the chart diagnosis.
distractorExplanations.b: Starts from the problem list; strengths practice looks first at what the client already uses, then addresses barriers.
distractorExplanations.c: Starts from the expert model; strengths practice treats the client as the expert on their own resources and goals.

aswb-bachelors-readiness-check-hgb-009.prompt: Clients at a county benefits office wait six hours, then lose SNAP when an online portal rejects hyphenated names. When the BSW documents this barrier, which level of oppression fits?

options.a: Macro-level policy and structural barriers in public systems
options.b: One clerk's biased remark to a single applicant that morning
options.c: Family household rules that restrict one member's spending
options.d: Informal norms on one unit's Monday morning staffing huddle

aswb-bachelors-readiness-check-hgb-009.explanation: Wait-time design and a portal that cannot handle hyphenated names are structural, policy-level barriers (macro). Person-in-environment practice names those systems so advocacy is not reduced to coaching one client to be more patient with a broken process.

distractorExplanations.b: Places the harm at the micro level of one remark; portal design and wait rules are institutional, not a single clerk's comment.
distractorExplanations.c: Places the harm inside one household; SNAP portal rules are public-system structures, not family money rules.
distractorExplanations.d: Places the harm at the mezzo level of one team; county-wide portal and wait design operate above a single huddle.

aswb-bachelors-readiness-check-hgb-010.prompt: A high-school BSW sees a 16-year-old referred after a fight. The student is quiet about home, friends, and substances. Which screening focus fits generalist adolescent risk assessment?

options.a: An IQ battery and statewide achievement percentiles before any talk
options.b: Safety, substance use, and available adult supports in the network
options.c: Projective drawings and dream content as the first interview tasks
options.d: An adult personality-disorder checklist completed in this visit

aswb-bachelors-readiness-check-hgb-010.explanation: Generalist adolescent risk screening (HEADSS-style) asks about home, safety, substances, and supports. A school or agency BSW uses direct, developmentally fit questions; IQ testing, projectives, and personality-disorder checklists are not the first-line risk screen and overreach BSW scope.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses risk screening with psychological evaluation; IQ and achievement scores do not answer safety, substances, or supports.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses risk screening with projective techniques reserved for trained clinicians; first-line screening uses direct safety questions.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses adolescent screening with adult personality-disorder diagnosis, which is not a BSW first-line risk tool before 18.

aswb-bachelors-readiness-check-hgb-011.prompt: A hospital BSW meets an adult whose partner died four months ago. The client works most days, then has waves of crying and sleep disruption without suicidal intent. How should the BSW frame this grief?

options.a: A required five-stage sequence that must finish in a fixed order
options.b: A process that is resolved for most people within two full weeks
options.c: A wavy, non-linear process rather than a fixed five-step homework
options.d: Complicated grief solely because it has lasted past one calendar month

aswb-bachelors-readiness-check-hgb-011.explanation: Typical grief after a death is often wavy—waves of yearning, work, and sleep change—rather than a required Kübler-Ross sequence. Four months of functioning with intermittent distress is still within a common bereavement range; the BSW normalizes, screens safety, and does not treat duration past one month as a diagnosis by itself.

distractorExplanations.a: Misreads Kübler-Ross as a required order; grief usually moves back and forth rather than through five assigned steps.
distractorExplanations.b: Uses a two-week depressive-episode window as if it were a grief deadline; ordinary grief often lasts months with waves.
distractorExplanations.d: Sets a one-month complicated-grief cutoff that does not match adult prolonged-grief timeframes; duration alone at one month is not the rule.

aswb-bachelors-readiness-check-hgb-012.prompt: A school BSW walks a building with a student who uses a wheelchair. Several classrooms sit up a stairwell, and the elevator is often locked. Using a social model of disability, what is the primary problem?

options.a: A medical condition that must be cured before the student can belong
options.b: A personal tragedy the student should overcome through private grit
options.c: An eligibility label used only to open a benefits or IEP file
options.d: Environmental and attitudinal barriers that keep the student out

aswb-bachelors-readiness-check-hgb-012.explanation: The social model locates disability in environmental and attitudinal barriers—locked elevators, stair-only rooms—not in the student's body as a failure to be cured. A school BSW's HBSE task is to name and reduce those barriers so participation is possible.

distractorExplanations.a: Describes the medical model; curing the body first is not how the social model explains exclusion from classrooms.
distractorExplanations.b: Describes the tragedy/charity model; asking for private grit ignores locked elevators the school controls.
distractorExplanations.c: Describes an administrative eligibility definition; the social model is about barriers, not a benefits label.

aswb-bachelors-readiness-check-hgb-013.prompt: After an eviction notice, a client at family services says usual coping has collapsed and they cannot think past tonight, though the worker has seen harsher housing crises. How is crisis defined for this BSW?

options.a: The client's experience that usual coping is overwhelmed right now
options.b: How severe an outsider rates the triggering event on a checklist
options.c: Whether acute stress disorder criteria are fully met on a form
options.d: The worker's numeric danger score on the agency safety sheet

aswb-bachelors-readiness-check-hgb-013.explanation: Crisis theory defines crisis by the person's experience that usual coping has failed, not by how dramatic the event looks to the worker. The BSW starts where the client is, then adds safety steps. A DSM label or the worker's calm comparison does not decide whether the client is in crisis.

distractorExplanations.b: Rates the event from outside; crisis is the client's overwhelmed coping, not an observer's severity ranking of eviction.
distractorExplanations.c: Treats crisis as a DSM skill; acute stress disorder is a clinical diagnosis and is not required to name a crisis state.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses danger scoring with the definition of crisis; risk numbers guide safety, but crisis is the client's overwhelmed coping.

aswb-bachelors-readiness-check-hgb-014.prompt: In a hospital ED a young adult is accompanied by an older companion who answers every question, holds the client's ID, and will not leave the room. What is the most accurate trafficking-informed observation for the BSW?

options.a: Undocumented status by itself is enough to prove trafficking today
options.b: A controlling companion plus missing documents is a red-flag cluster
options.c: A large age gap in the pair is enough by itself to confirm trafficking
options.d: Any out-of-state travel for work is itself a trafficking indicator

aswb-bachelors-readiness-check-hgb-014.explanation: Red flags cluster around control: someone else speaking, holding identity documents, and blocking private conversation. The BSW follows hospital protocol for private screening and reporting pathways rather than confronting or attempting a freelance rescue. Immigration status, age gap, or travel alone is not proof.

distractorExplanations.a: Treats immigration status as diagnostic; status can raise vulnerability but is not itself an indicator of trafficking.
distractorExplanations.c: Treats an age gap as confirmation; age difference alone is not a trafficking indicator without control and coercion signs.
distractorExplanations.d: Treats ordinary work travel as a red flag; movement is concerning when someone else controls papers, money, and speech.

aswb-bachelors-readiness-check-hgb-015.prompt: A community-clinic BSW meets a parent who started opioid use after a work injury, lost a job, and now uses with friends. Staff argue it is only willpower. What is the most accurate HBSE frame?

options.a: Addiction is only a moral failure of individual willpower to stop
options.b: Addiction is only a brain disease with no social or family context
options.c: Addiction as a biopsychosocial pattern of body, mind, and setting
options.d: Addiction is treated only with insight-oriented psychotherapy protocols

aswb-bachelors-readiness-check-hgb-015.explanation: HBSE treats substance use as biopsychosocial: injury and pain (bio), coping and mood (psycho), job loss and using networks (social). A BSW case-manages medical care, supports, and environment; moralizing, brain-only models, or launching LCSW-style insight protocols miss that frame.

distractorExplanations.a: Reduces use to a moral willpower failure; that ignores injury, pain, job loss, and using networks the BSW must assess.
distractorExplanations.b: Reduces use to a brain-only disease; HBSE still includes social setting, employment, and family context around the biology.
distractorExplanations.d: Turns the item into an LCSW therapy protocol; generalist practice uses a biopsychosocial case-management frame, not insight therapy as the skill.
